group.passage: In most countries, a family name is handed down from parents to children. Iceland does things differently. Below, a language writer explains how Icelandic last names work, and an Icelander living in Canada describes what happens when her name travels abroad.

passage_parts.label: A
passage_parts.title: Names That Change Every Generation
passage_parts.text: Most Icelanders have no family name in the usual sense. Instead, a person’s last name comes from the first name of a parent, usually the father, followed by -son for a son or -dóttir for a daughter. If a man named Gunnar has a son called Einar and a daughter called Helga, they will be Einar Gunnarsson and Helga Gunnarsdóttir, and Einar’s own children will in turn be Einarsson or Einarsdóttir. A last name therefore reveals who someone’s parent is rather than which family they belong to, and it does not change when its owner marries. Names based on a mother’s first name are possible too, and they have become more common. Because last names shift with every generation, even telephone directories are arranged by first name. Given names, in contrast, follow strict rules: any new one needs the approval of a naming committee, and one that cannot take the endings of Icelandic grammar is usually turned down.

passage_parts.label: B
passage_parts.title: My Name Abroad
passage_parts.text: When I moved to Canada, I never imagined that my name would need so much explaining. I am Sigrún Ólafsdóttir, which simply means that my father is called Ólafur. My son, however, is Ari Sigrúnarson, because my husband and I wanted him to carry my name. On our first trip abroad together, an airport officer looked closely at our passports and asked, quite seriously, whether Ari was really my child. I felt so embarrassed that I could hardly answer, and ever since, I have carried a copy of his birth certificate whenever we travel. At work, colleagues used to call me “Ms. Ólafsdóttir”, which sounded as if they were speaking to my father’s daughter rather than to me. Back home, nobody would address me that way. Still, I would never trade my name for a family name. It ties me to my father, just as Ari’s name ties him to me, and that link means the world to me.

translation_zh.text:
在大多數國家，家族姓氏由父母傳給子女。冰島的做法不一樣。下面，一位語言作家說明冰島人的姓是怎麼來的，一位住在加拿大的冰島人則描述她的名字到了國外會發生什麼事。

A　每一代都會改變的姓
大多數冰島人沒有一般意義上的家族姓氏。一個人的姓，是取父母其中一人（通常是父親）的名字，兒子加上 -son、女兒加上 -dóttir。如果一位名叫 Gunnar 的男子有個兒子叫 Einar、女兒叫 Helga，他們就會是 Einar Gunnarsson 和 Helga Gunnarsdóttir，而 Einar 自己的孩子則會姓 Einarsson 或 Einarsdóttir。因此，一個人的姓顯示的是他的父母是誰，而不是他屬於哪個家族，而且姓的主人結婚時也不會改變。以母親名字構成的姓也可以，而且越來越普遍。由於姓氏每一代都會變，連電話簿都是依名字排列。相較之下，名字則有嚴格的規定：任何新名字都需要命名委員會的核准，不能套用冰島語語法字尾的名字通常會被駁回。

B　我的名字在國外
搬到加拿大時，我從沒想到我的名字需要這麼多解釋。我叫 Sigrún Ólafsdóttir，意思很簡單，就是我的父親叫 Ólafur。不過，我的兒子叫 Ari Sigrúnarson，因為我和先生希望他帶著我的名字。我們第一次一起出國時，一位機場人員仔細看了我們的護照，一本正經地問 Ari 真的是我的孩子嗎。我尷尬得幾乎答不出話來；從那以後，只要出門旅行，我都會帶著他的出生證明影本。在公司，同事以前總叫我「Ólafsdóttir 女士」，聽起來好像他們是在跟我父親的女兒說話，而不是在跟我說話。在冰島，沒有人會這樣稱呼我。儘管如此，我絕不會拿我的名字去換一個家族姓氏。它把我和父親連在一起，就像 Ari 的名字把他和我連在一起，而這份連結對我來說無比珍貴。
